title: Ultrasonic Testing for Pipelines | UT Inspection (US)
description: On-site ultrasonic testing for US gas and liquids pipelines: dig thickness grids, station piping and weld checks. Mobilized to your site. Request a UT quote.
h1: Ultrasonic Pipeline Inspection: UT Thickness and Weld Testing for US Pipelines
html:
Atlantis NDT performs on-site ultrasonic testing on United States gas and hazardous-liquid pipelines: wall thickness grids at integrity digs, thickness checks on station piping, and manual angle-beam examination of repair and tie-in welds. Technicians are mobilized to the right-of-way, the dig or the station for the agreed scope. Send the pipe size, wall, grade, the anomaly list and the governing code, and request a UT inspection quote.

Where ultrasonic pipeline inspection fits in an integrity program

Most buried transmission and gathering pipe is first examined from the inside by in-line tools run by the operator or a specialist vendor. Atlantis does not run in-line tools. Our ultrasonic work starts after that: once the operator selects anomalies to excavate, someone has to confirm what is actually in the ground, and a hand-held ultrasonic thickness reading is the most direct way to do it. The operator compares our readings with the tool report and decides whether the tool is performing as specified.

The same method supports above-ground assets that are never piggable: compressor and pump station piping, meter and regulator runs, scraper launchers and receivers, relief headers and short tie-ins. Those assets sit under the same federal framework as the line pipe, so the examination record has to be traceable to a procedure, an instrument and a qualified technician. This page covers what we examine, which US rules drive the work, how the technique is applied on pipe, and what you receive. If you are comparing methods, our magnetic particle work on pipelines and liquid penetrant work on pipelines cover surface cracking, which ultrasonic thickness readings do not detect.

The US rules behind the examination

Gas transmission and gathering pipe falls under PHMSA 49 CFR Part 192, hazardous-liquid pipe under 49 CFR Part 195. Both parts require welds to be examined to an accepted standard and both contain integrity management provisions for pipe in high-consequence areas, which is why dig verification is such a common job. Design and repair practice is usually written around ASME B31.8 for gas and ASME B31.4 for liquids, and pipeline girth welds are qualified and accepted to API 1104. Station piping may be designed to one of those codes or to ASME B31.3, so we ask which one applies before we choose reference levels and acceptance wording.

Operator qualification matters too. Subpart N of Part 192 and Subpart G of Part 195 require operators to qualify people who perform covered tasks. Whether a given inspection task is a covered task depends on the operator’s written plan, so we ask for the plan’s requirements when we quote and confirm before we mobilize. Our technicians work under the company written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A: Level II technicians perform and interpret examinations, and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports.

What we examine at the dig

An integrity dig exposes a short length of pipe, usually a few feet to a few tens of feet, after the operator has removed the coating. Once the steel is cleaned, we examine the area the in-line tool flagged and the pipe around it. Typical items are:

  • Metal-loss anomalies. We lay out a grid over the corroded area, record a thickness at each node, and report the minimum, the nominal wall and the extent. The grid spacing is set by the operator’s procedure and the size of the feature.
  • Laminations and wall variations. Straight-beam scanning across a marked band shows whether a feature the tool called metal loss is actually a lamination or an inclusion in the pipe body.
  • Dents and mechanical damage. Thickness readings across a dent show wall change; the surface of a dent also needs a crack check, which is a magnetic particle job rather than an ultrasonic one.
  • Seam and girth weld areas. Corrosion is often worse along a seam or beside a girth weld, so the grid is extended across the weld and the readings on either side are recorded separately.
  • Sleeves and repair fittings. Wall thickness under and beside installed sleeves, fittings and welded repairs, where access allows.

The numbers go to the operator’s integrity engineer. Atlantis does not calculate remaining life, set reassessment intervals or perform fitness-for-service analysis; those decisions belong to the operator’s engineer or qualified inspector, working from our data.

Technique on line pipe

Thickness gauging on pipe uses a dual-element probe for rough, pitted surfaces or a single-element probe where the surface is smooth. The instrument is calibrated on a step block of the same acoustic velocity as the pipe steel, usually carbon steel in an API 5L grade, and the calibration is checked at the start of the shift, at intervals, and whenever the probe or setup changes. Reference practice follows ASME Section V, Article 5 for ultrasonic thickness measurement, and our guide to Article 5 thickness measurement requirements explains what the code expects from the procedure.

Surface condition decides data quality. Coating remnants, mill scale and corrosion product reduce coupling and bias readings, so the operator’s excavation crew removes the coating and we dress a clean path on the pipe. On warm pipe in summer or on a line that is running hot, a high-temperature couplant is selected and the instrument is calibrated at a temperature close to the test surface. Cold-weather digs need a couplant that stays workable and a probe that has been kept warm between readings, otherwise the first readings of the day drift.

The pipeline-specific limit is geometry. On small-diameter or heavily curved surfaces the probe face rocks, so we use a curved-shoe probe or lay out the grid so each reading is taken on a short flat dressed spot. Wall readings at 6 o’clock on a line that carries water or wet gas deserve extra grid density, because internal corrosion collects there. Where a reading does not repeat, we record both values and flag the point rather than average it away.

Weld examination with angle-beam ultrasonics

Ultrasonic weld inspection on pipe uses shear-wave probes of suitable angle, scanned from both sides of the weld where access allows. On pipeline repair work the main targets are tie-in girth welds, sleeve end fillets in thicker wall, and welds on branch and fitting connections. Acceptance depends on the governing document: for girth welds that is API 1104 and the operator’s specification, and for station piping it is the construction code. We report indications against the criteria the operator names. For general weld examination detail see our page on ultrasonic weld inspection.

For new-construction girth welds, many operators specify radiography or fully mechanized systems. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States and does not offer those mechanized systems; if your specification calls for them, you will need a licensed contractor for that part. We can support the project with manual ultrasonic work on repairs and tie-ins where your procedure allows it, and with reviews of the contractor’s procedures by an ASNT Level III.

Which method for which pipeline question

Choosing between UT, MT and PT on pipeline items
QuestionUsual methodWhy
How thick is the wall under this metal-loss anomaly?UT thickness gridReads remaining wall directly; no surface crack sensitivity needed
Is there cracking at a dent, gouge or weld toe?MT on carbon steelSensitive to tight surface cracks on ferromagnetic pipe
Is a stainless or non-ferrous station component cracked?PTMT does not work on non-magnetic metal
Is a lamination present in the pipe body?UT straight beamPlanar flaws parallel to the surface reflect sound
Is a repair weld sound through its thickness?UT angle beamReaches embedded flaws; surface methods only see the surface

What the report contains

Every ultrasonic examination is documented so another qualified person can reproduce it. A typical report lists:

  • Operator, line or station name, pipe or component identification, dig or work-order number and the location of the examination.
  • Pipe size, nominal wall, grade and seam type as supplied by the operator.
  • The written procedure used, its revision, and the edition of the code behind it.
  • Instrument, probe, couplant, calibration block and the calibration check results.
  • Technician name, SNT-TC-1A level and the Level III who approved the procedure.
  • The thickness grid with the minimum reading highlighted, or the indication list with location, length, amplitude and the criterion applied.
  • A sketch or marked photograph tied to a clock position and a dimension from a named weld or marker.
  • Acceptance wording only where the operator has named the criteria; otherwise the report states the readings and the reference level without disposition.

What to send for a quote

  1. Pipe diameter, wall, grade, seam type and operating temperature.
  2. The anomaly or component list, with dig numbers and expected exposure dates.
  3. Governing code and edition, plus the operator’s procedure if one exists.
  4. Coating type and who removes it.
  5. Access conditions: trench shoring, confined space, traffic control, landowner or permitting limits.
  6. Site orientation, badging and any operator qualification requirements.
  7. Site address, contact and the report format you prefer.

Planning realities on US pipelines

Digs are scheduled around coating crews, welders and hydrotest windows, and the ultrasonic work is a short block inside a longer sequence. We ask for the sequence in advance so we mobilize when the steel is clean and the engineer is ready for the numbers. Open trenches bring their own hazards: shoring, atmospheric monitoring where gas may be present, and traffic control on roadway crossings. Work at stations adds permits, lockout, hot-work rules and escort requirements. We follow the operator’s site rules and do not start until the work area is released. Winter work in the northern plains and Rockies needs heated enclosures or thermal blankets for couplant and instruments, and wet clay soils can make dig access slow.

Where we work in the United States

Pipeline work follows the pipe, not a single hub. These city pages describe how we mobilize into each corridor:

  • Houston: Gulf Coast gathering, transmission and terminal piping feeding the Ship Channel refineries.
  • Tulsa: mid-continent liquids and gas lines with long-established integrity programs.
  • Midland: Permian gathering and takeaway lines carrying sour and wet streams.
  • Oklahoma City: Anadarko Basin gathering and compressor stations.
  • Kansas City: interstate gas corridors crossing Kansas and Missouri.
  • Denver: DJ Basin and Rockies gathering with cold-weather digging.
  • Shreveport: Haynesville gas gathering and higher-pressure transmission.
  • Pittsburgh: Appalachian midstream lines and compressor sites in steep terrain.
  • Omaha: Midwest transmission and liquids lines across river and rail crossings.

What we do not do on pipelines

We do not run in-line inspection tools, we do not perform radiography in the United States, and we do not calculate remaining life or intervals. Specialist techniques for crack depth sizing or long-range screening are outside this page. For a broader look at pipeline scopes see pipeline inspection services, and for piping circuits inside stations see piping circuit inspection and CML thickness surveys.

Training your own technicians

Operators that want in-house thickness gauging can build the skill through UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, with simulator practice in Practical NDT ultrasonic simulator. Industry-specific coursework is on the pipeline NDT training page. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its own personnel, so we help you write the practice rather than issue the certificate. See written practice development.

faq.q: What does ultrasonic pipeline inspection actually measure at a dig?
faq.a: It measures the remaining wall thickness of the steel at each point on a grid, and where flaws exist parallel to the surface it can show laminations. The readings let the operator’s engineer compare ground truth with what the in-line tool reported.

faq.q: Do you run in-line inspection tools or interpret their data?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not run in-line tools. We take hand-held ultrasonic readings after the operator excavates, and the operator or its tool vendor compares those readings with the in-line report.

faq.q: Can you inspect pipe that is in service?
faq.a: Yes, thickness readings can be taken on pipe that is operating, provided the surface is clean, the temperature is within the couplant and probe range, and the operator releases the work area. Welding and repair decisions remain with the operator.

faq.q: Which codes and regulators govern this work?
faq.a: Gas lines fall under PHMSA 49 CFR Part 192 and liquid lines under Part 195, with ASME B31.8 and B31.4 as the usual design codes and API 1104 for girth welds. Station piping may be written to ASME B31.3, so we confirm the code before we set up.

faq.q: Who decides whether a wall reading or indication is acceptable?
faq.a: The operator decides, through its engineer or qualified inspector. We report readings and indications against the criteria the operator names, and we state the reference level and procedure so the engineer can evaluate the result.

faq.q: What do you need from us to quote a pipeline UT job?
faq.a: Pipe size, wall, grade and seam type, the anomaly or component list, the governing code and edition, coating removal responsibility, access and permit conditions, and the site address. A procedure or earlier report helps if one exists.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic thickness testing find cracks at a dent or weld?
faq.a: Thickness readings do not find tight surface cracks. For dents, gouges and weld toes on carbon steel, magnetic particle inspection is the usual surface check, and we can pair the two on the same dig.

faq.q: How do you handle operator qualification requirements?
faq.a: We ask the operator how its written plan treats NDT tasks and confirm before mobilizing. Where the plan requires an evaluation we do not hold, the operator’s own qualified person performs that covered task and we support with the examination data.

faq.q: Do you inspect new-construction girth welds?
faq.a: We do not perform radiography in the United States and do not offer fully mechanized systems. We can perform manual angle-beam examination on repairs and tie-ins where your procedure allows it, and an ASNT Level III can review the contractor’s procedures.
